owner.occupation: Staff nurse at a public hospital

world.bio: Staff nurse at a public hospital in Kuala Lumpur, mostly nights on the medical ward. I am Malaysian Chinese, I read Chinese but speak it with a Cantonese lilt, which makes my mother laugh. My family has worked the Selayang wholesale market for three generations, though I took the hospital road. On days off I bake kaya puffs and give them away to the ward.
skills_assets: Registered nurse, twelve years on medical and surgical wards
Fluent in English, Malay, Cantonese and Mandarin; reads simplified and traditional Chinese
Family connections in the Selayang wholesale market through uncles and cousins
Kaya puff and pineapple tart recipes from her grandmother, small home-baking oven
Volunteers at a temple food bank on Sunday mornings

projects.name: Son's Taiwan university fund
projects.text: Saving monthly so that my son can study in Taiwan after high school. He is fifteen, wants engineering, and keeps asking when we start looking at school lists. I put away RM 1,500 a month, not enough yet.

projects.name: Mother's diabetes care
projects.text: Mother has type 2 diabetes. I take her for check-ups every two months and keep her food diary. She cheats with kuih.

notes.text: Night shift, quiet. Mr. Tan in Bed 6 asked me to read his daughter's WeChat voice message because his eyes are too bad. She said she would visit on Sunday. He smiled for the whole night.
Baked 60 kaya puffs. Half went to the ward, half to my neighbour who just had a baby. My son ate seven. Grandma's recipe still works, though the oven runs hot.
Mother's HbA1c is up again. She says it is the stress of Cousin Ah Seng's business. I told her it is the kuih. She laughed, which means I am right.

Selayang market visit on my day off. Uncle was unloading durians. Ah Seng was at his fruit-import stall, complaining as usual that the Chinese navel oranges reach him through two middlemen and by the time they get to him the margin is almost nothing. I told him I know nothing about oranges, only about hospitals. He said you know people. I said I know patients.
Temple food bank Sunday. Forty families this week, up from thirty-five. Packed rice, cooking oil and tinned sardines. An old lady asked if I could bring vegetables next time. Will ask my uncle.
Wrote to a friend in Taipei about the Taiwan university route for my son. Fees, scholarships, the dormitory. She said start early. I said we are early. She said no you are not.
Was woken by my son asking about maths. I teach nursing, I do not do calculus. We worked through it together. He grinned at the end. A good day.
Double-shifted. Fell asleep at the traffic light. Honked at by a Grab driver. Need to take real leave, but who covers.

messages.text: Ah Seng: Siew Ling, you free this weekend? Me: Why? Ah Seng: My stall is a mess, the oranges are at the same price as last month but my supplier raised again. Me: Who is your supplier? Ah Seng: A guy in Klang who buys from another guy. Me: That is two middlemen. Ah Seng: Exactly.
Mother: Did you take your lunch? Me: I'm on the ward. Mother: Eat. Me: I will. Mother: Your brother's wife sent kuih. Me: I know you ate it.
Jun Wei: Ma, can I apply for Taiwan scholarships? Me: Yes, we start looking next month. Jun Wei: I need a laptop. Me: We will see. Jun Wei: Ma. Me: We will see.
Mdm. Lee: Can you come early on Sunday? Me: What time? Mdm. Lee: Seven. Me: I'll be post-night shift. Mdm. Lee: Come anyway, we will give you tea.
Friend: Visit in March? Me: Maybe. Friend: Bring your son. Me: I will think.

relations.about: Runs a fruit-import stall at Selayang, always tired, always complaining about prices.
Seventy, diabetic, lives in Jinjang, sharp-tongued.
Still sells vegetables at the market, knows everybody.

constraints: Cannot take more than two days of leave at a time
Savings target for her son's tuition, not touching it
Does not like to push business at family gatherings
Works nights, so mornings are for sleep
sensitive: Worries she is too tired to be a good mother
Husband left five years ago; she rarely mentions it
